lead: A physiological transducer turns a body variable — force, pressure, temperature or light — into an electrical signal that a recorder can read. The load cell is the common force version: a metal element bends under load, strain gauges change resistance, and a Wheatstone bridge turns that tiny change into millivolts. You meet it in weighing scales, hospital beds, infusion pumps and gait force plates. This chapter explains how to choose a transducer, compares five transducer families, and follows one quarter-bridge load cell from 1000 µε to 2.5 mV.
prereq: You need basic circuit laws and the Wheatstone bridge; bio-signal origin is in Chapter 1.1 and electrode matching in Chapter 1.2.

blocks.text: Selection criteria. A physiological transducer must not disturb the body and must give a usable electrical copy of the variable. Its range is the smallest to largest input it can measure without damage. Sensitivity is output change per unit input, for example 2 mV per 100 g. Linearity says the sensitivity stays constant over the range. Hysteresis is the difference between readings when you increase and then decrease the input; a good transducer has little hysteresis. Accuracy is closeness to the true value. Resolution is the smallest change it can show. Loading effect is the disturbance the transducer itself causes: a stiff force sensor takes load from tissue, a cold probe cools skin. Biocompatibility means the material touching the patient is safe and cleanable. Range and accuracy should match the clinical question; an extra digit of resolution is useless if hysteresis is large. Some syllabi call this physiological transducers and selection criteria.

The main families differ in what changes. A resistive transducer changes resistance with strain, temperature or light; the strain gauge is one. A capacitive transducer changes capacitance when plates move or the dielectric changes; it suits small displacement and pressure. An inductive transducer changes inductance through a moving core, useful for displacement. A piezoelectric crystal gives charge when squeezed; it measures dynamic force and vibration, not steady weight because charge leaks away. A photoelectric transducer changes current with light; it appears in pulse oximetry and optical counting. An electrochemical transducer converts a chemical concentration into voltage or current; glucose sensors use it, covered in Unit 4, biosensors. Temperature sensors are a short comparison: a thermistor is resistive and sensitive but nonlinear; an RTD is resistive and stable; a thermocouple is a small voltage from two metals and needs cold-junction correction. Choose the family by the variable, the bandwidth and the loading the body can tolerate.
A strain gauge is a thin metal or semiconductor foil bonded to a spring element. When the element stretches, the foil lengthens and narrows, so its resistance rises.

blocks.where: GF is the gauge factor, dimensionless; ΔR is the change in resistance in Ω; R is the unstrained resistance in Ω; ε is strain, the fractional change in length, dimensionless.

blocks.text: Metal foil gauges have GF near 2; semiconductor gauges are higher but more temperature-sensitive. Four gauges make a load cell. In a quarter bridge one gauge is active. In a half bridge two gauges are active, one in tension and one in compression. In a full bridge all four are active.

blocks.where: ΔV is the bridge output in V for a quarter bridge; V<sub>ex</sub> is the excitation voltage in V; GF is the gauge factor; ε is strain.

blocks.text: A half bridge gives twice this output, a full bridge four times. A load cell has a machined beam, column or diaphragm; gauges are bonded and sealed; a full bridge is usual. Its output is quoted in mV/V, so it scales with excitation. Load cells weigh patients, medicines and food, and force platforms use them in gait and balance studies (see Chapter 1.11). The next stage is the bio-amplifier and ADC (see Chapter 1.4).

examples.question: A quarter-bridge load cell uses 350 Ω strain gauges, excitation 5 V and gauge factor 2.0. The strain is 1000 µε (1×10⁻³). Find the bridge output in volts and millivolts.
steps: Given: V_ex = 5 V, GF = 2.0, ε = 1000 µε.
Use the quarter-bridge formula: ΔV = V_ex × GF × ε / 4.
examples.answer: The bridge output is 0.0025 V, which is 2.5 mV.
examples.check:
V_ex = 5.0
GF = 2.0
epsilon = 1000e-6
delta_v = V_ex * GF * epsilon / 4
delta_mv = delta_v * 1000
print(f"{delta_v:.4f}")
print(f"{delta_mv:.1f}")

traps: In a quarter bridge only one gauge is active, so its output is one quarter of a full bridge for the same strain; a half bridge is one half.
Convert microstrain to strain before using the formula: 1000 µε = 1×10⁻³, not 1000.
A load cell's millivolt output depends on excitation voltage; doubling V_ex doubles the output, so a reading without V_ex is incomplete.
High sensitivity is not the same as high accuracy; hysteresis, linearity and loading effect can dominate.
Piezoelectric sensors measure dynamic force, not steady weight; do not use them for a static load cell question.

quiz.a: A device that converts a body variable such as force, pressure or temperature into an electrical signal.

quiz.q: State the gauge factor formula and define its symbols.
quiz.a: GF = (ΔR/R)/ε; ΔR is the resistance change, R is the unstrained resistance, and ε is strain.

quiz.q: Why does a full bridge give four times the quarter-bridge output for the same strain?
quiz.a: All four gauges are active: two in tension and two in compression, so their resistance changes add in the bridge instead of one change acting alone.

quiz.q: A quarter-bridge load cell has V_ex = 10 V, GF = 2.0 and ε = 500 µε. Find the output.
Using the worked example's load cell, find the output if the bridge is changed to a half bridge.
quiz.a: A half bridge doubles the quarter-bridge output: 2 × 2.5 mV = 5.0 mV.

quiz.q: A force sensor has high sensitivity but large hysteresis. Why may it be a poor choice for gait measurement?
quiz.a: Gait force rises and falls repeatedly; hysteresis makes the loading and unloading curves differ, so the same force reads differently, and high sensitivity cannot fix that error.

quiz.q: Why is a piezoelectric transducer unsuitable for weighing a patient who lies still?
quiz.a: It gives charge only while force changes; a steady load leaks away, so it cannot hold a stable reading.

quiz.q: A force sensor has range 0–2000 N, resolution 1 N and accuracy ±10 N. Which specification should you quote for error?
quiz.a: Accuracy dominates: resolution 1 N is finer than ±10 N, so quote ±10 N, not 1 N.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern load cells often add a digital interface and temperature compensation inside the housing, so the amplifier sees a calibrated digital value. MEMS piezoresistive gauges put a force sensor on a chip for catheters and wearable devices. Force plates in gait labs use multiple load cells to report centre of pressure as well as total force. Search for strain gauge rosettes, load cell mV/V calibration, and force platform centre of pressure.
